full_judgment:
2. The point that falls for determination by this Court in this case is whether the lower appellate Court committed an error of law in its decision in dismissing the pre-emption case holding that the case is not maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 on the finding that the land under pre-emption is not an agricultural land. 

 3. The petitioner instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1977 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-empting the land in question on the plea that Bidhyadar Mondal, the owner of the land, sold it to the opposite party Nos. 1-3 who were strangers to the holding and the petitioner is the contiguous owner by purchase. The opposite-party Nos. 1-3 resisted the case on the ground that it was not maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the land was Bhiti as recorded in both CS and SA khatians. The trial Court allowed pre-emption case. Against that judgment and order the opposite party Nos. 1-3 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 374 of 1979 which was allowed and the pre-emption case was dismissed by the impugned judgment and order. 

 4. Mr. Fazlul Karim submits that the land which is recorded as Bhiti land is being used for the purpose of cultivation and is connected with agriculture and as such it is not a non-agricultural land. He says that by subsequent use for the purpose of agricultural or horticultural, although a but stands on it, the land has changed its nature to agricultural land. Placing reliance upon section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act he submits that as the disputed land was connected with agricultural operation it is agricultural land. In this context he also placed reliance upon the following observation in the decision in the case of Dulichand Mehesriand and others Vs. Prohlad Chandra and others 1945 Cal. 50 "The requirements of section 182 would be satisfied if the homestead was one from which the raiyat might, if necessary, carry on agricultural operation in his raiyati holding, if and when the occasion arose." The fact of the case is distinguishable from the facts of the present case. There the lease of the shop was taken for the purpose of business. In view of the facts of that case, I think, the principle laid down therein has little application to the facts of the present case. Moreover, the decision was given in a quite different context on interpretation of section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Mr. Karim further cites the decision in the case of M/s Lutfun Nahar Vs. Syeeda Hasmat Ara Begum and another 21 DLR 633 wherein it has been held that the purpose of lease and the document creating the lease are determinant factors as to whether the land is agricultural or non-agricultural land. In that case in the document creating the lease it was stated that the lessee shall be at liberty to construct pucca building. On construction of the document the learned Judge held that the tenancy originally was created for homestead. This case is also of no help to the petitioner as in the instant case there is nothing to show that the vendor of the petitioner obtained the lease for agricultural purpose. Mr. Karim placed reliance upon the decision in the case of Akbar Ali and others Vs. Zahiruddin Kari and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81 wherein it has been held that according to section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in a record of right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect and a part of the holding of a raiyat is not excluded from the operation of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. I fail to understand how this case helps Mr. Karim as in the record of right, the CS khatian and the S.A. Khatian, the disputed land has been recorded as "Bhiti" meaning non-agricultural land. 

 5. Mr. Karim also refers to the recital of the kabala to argue that the land is an agricultural land as the kabala describes the land as "Chashi-Bhiti". He further invited my attention to the statement of DW 1 in cross-examination and other witnesses to show that their statements also support the recital and contends that the land is an agricultural land. This contention has no substance. The avocation or occupation of a tenant does not determine the character of the land. It is the purpose for which the lease is taken that determines the nature of the land. 

 7. Mr. NK Shaha, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, submits that the court of appeal below correctly held on the basis of both CS and SA khatian that the holding is non-agricultural one. Mr. Shaha also submits that the initial purpose for which the lease is grated determines the character of the land and not the subsequent use. It is a well-settled principle of law that the initial purpose for which the lease is created determines the nature of the land and not the subsequent user of it. Mr. Shaha rebutted the contention of Mr. Karim that the land is an agricultural one as the lessee and the witnesses are agriculturists and from the "Bhiti" the lessee carries on agricultural operation by contending that merely because the witnesses and the lessees are agriculturists the land does not fall within the meaning of agricultural land and it does not lose its original nature. He relied upon the decision in the case of Kamini Sundari Majhi Vs. Meseruddin Sheikh and others PLR 1960 Dac. 1018 wherein Murshed, J held that where the land is not used for cultivation the petitioner (Pre-emptor) does not come within the definition of raiyat within the meaning of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This decision applies to the facts of the present case. In the instant case there is no finding that the lease was taken for agricultural purpose. On the contrary, it is found that the land is a "Bhiti" meaning non-agricultural land. This entry cannot be wiped out merely on the basis of a recital in the deed describing the land as a "Chashi-Bhiti" land. Mr. Shaha also relied upon the case of Forman All Howlader Vs. Helaluddin Pashari 20 DLR 1197 wherein it has been held that pre-emption in respect of Non-Agricultural land is only maintainable under section 24 of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and not under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Although from the homestead standing on the disputed land the agricultural operation is carried out but that ipso facto does not change the nature of the land. Mere recital in the deed describing the character of the land under pre-emption as agricultural one does not also change the character of the land against the entry in CS khatians recording the disputed land as "Bhiti" which evidently indicates that the purpose for which the lease was taken was not agricultural one.
